title: PRSL-AI-Ecosystem
description: PRSL-AI Ecosystem & iRiel AI  Architecture, Normative Requirements, and Future Intent  Organization: Robert Software Labs Ecosystem: PRSL-AI Intelligence Platform: iRiel AI Document Type: Architecture and Requirements Specification Version: 1.1 Status: Proposed Baseline  ⸻  1. Purpose and Scope  This document defines the architectural relationship between PRSL-AI and iRiel AI, establishes normative requirements for their design and implementation, and identifies future capabilities that remain subject to planning and verification.  It separates three categories:  1. Normative requirements: Conditions that implementations must satisfy when the applicable requirements are adopted. 2. Architectural guidance: Recommended design practices that support maintainability, interoperability, and security. 3. Future intent: Proposed capabilities and strategic objectives that are not commitments to current functionality.  This document does not, by itself, establish that any particular capability has been implemented, deployed, or independently verified.  2. Terminology and Requirement Language  The following terms are used normatively:  * MUST / MUST NOT: An absolute requirement or prohibition within the stated scope. * SHOULD / SHOULD NOT: A strong recommendation that may be departed from only for a documented reason. * MAY: An explicitly permitted option.  These terms distinguish requirements from preferences and future objectives.  A requirement is considered satisfied only when its implementation can be demonstrated through appropriate evidence, such as source code, automated tests, configuration, security controls, or documented integration behavior.  3. System Definition  3.1 PRSL-AI Ecosystem  PRSL-AI is the ecosystem-level architecture associated with Robert Software Labs.  Its defined architectural scope includes the relationship between participating projects, shared integration contracts, and ecosystem-level engineering principles.  3.2 iRiel AI  iRiel AI is the AI platform intended to provide intelligence-related capabilities to applications within the PRSL-AI ecosystem.  Its architectural scope includes model integration, intelligence orchestration, context management, and authorized tool interaction where these capabilities are implemented.  3.3 Relationship Between the Systems  PRSL-AI defines the ecosystem-level boundaries and standards. iRiel AI implements intelligence-platform capabilities within those boundaries.  This is a separation of architectural responsibilities, not a claim that every proposed ecosystem component or integration already exists.  ⸻  Part I — Normative Requirements  The requirements in this section define the proposed engineering baseline. They become binding implementation requirements when this specification is formally adopted for the relevant repositories or components.  4. Architectural Boundaries  REQ-ARCH-001 — Separation of Responsibilities  The implementation MUST maintain a documented separation between ecosystem-level responsibilities, intelligence-platform responsibilities, provider integrations, and application interfaces.  REQ-ARCH-002 — Explicit Interfaces  Subsystems MUST communicate through documented interfaces or contracts appropriate to their integration boundaries.  Implementations MUST NOT rely on undocumented cross-module behavior as a substitute for an explicit contract.  REQ-ARCH-003 — Dependency Direction  Dependencies between components MUST be intentional and documented. Provider-specific implementation details MUST NOT leak into unrelated core modules when an adapter boundary is defined for that integration.  REQ-ARCH-004 — Implementation Transparency  Documentation MUST distinguish implemented, partially implemented, planned, and unverified capabilities.  An architectural proposal MUST NOT be represented as evidence of an operational implementation.  5. Deterministic Execution and State  REQ-EXEC-001 — Explicit Control Flow  Where iRiel AI implements an execution engine, control flow MUST be explicit and inspectable.  Hidden recursion or implicit control-flow transitions MUST NOT replace a documented execution model.  REQ-EXEC-002 — State Transitions  State transitions MUST be defined through explicit rules. Where execution state is persisted or exposed for replay, its representation and transition semantics MUST be documented.  REQ-EXEC-003 — Execution Trace  The execution engine MUST expose sufficient structured information to reconstruct the sequence of observable execution steps, subject to privacy and security constraints.  Deterministic replay of model-generated behavior MUST NOT be assumed unless the relevant inputs, model outputs, tool results, and environmental dependencies are captured and controlled.  6. Provider Integration  REQ-PROV-001 — Provider Isolation  Each supported model provider MUST have a clearly defined integration boundary.  Provider-specific request and response handling MUST remain within the appropriate adapter or integration layer.  REQ-PROV-002 — Normalized Contracts  Provider adapters MUST normalize supported operations into documented platform-level contracts.  Unsupported capabilities MUST be reported explicitly rather than silently treated as equivalent to supported operations.  REQ-PROV-003 — Failure Propagation  Provider failures MUST be surfaced through documented error-handling mechanisms. Failures MUST NOT be silently discarded.  REQ-PROV-004 — Capability Verification  A provider integration MUST NOT advertise a capability as supported unless that capability has been implemented and verified for the relevant provider and configuration.  7. Tools, Permissions, and Validation  REQ-TOOL-001 — Input Validation  Tool inputs received from external or untrusted sources MUST be validated against the applicable input schema before execution.  REQ-TOOL-002 — Authorization  Tool execution MUST be subject to explicit authorization rules appropriate to the operation and its security impact.  REQ-TOOL-003 — Execution Controls  Where supported by the execution environment, tool operations MUST implement defined timeout and cancellation behavior.  Operations that cannot be safely cancelled MUST document their limitations.  REQ-TOOL-004 — Structured Outcomes  Tool execution MUST produce a documented success or failure outcome. Failures MUST retain sufficient structured context for diagnosis without unnecessarily exposing sensitive information.  REQ-TOOL-005 — Permission Enforcement  Permission checks MUST be enforced at the execution boundary. User-interface restrictions alone MUST NOT be treated as sufficient authorization for privileged operations.  8. Events and Streaming  REQ-EVENT-001 — Documented Event Contracts  Events exposed by the platform MUST have documented types, payloads, and semantics.  REQ-EVENT-002 — Ordering  The event system MUST define ordering guarantees for events within an execution. Where ordering cannot be guaranteed across concurrent operations, that limitation MUST be documented.  REQ-EVENT-003 — Error Events  Where an execution exposes structured events, relevant failures MUST be represented through the documented error mechanism and MUST NOT be silently swallowed.  REQ-EVENT-004 — Replay Guarantees  Replayable event streams MUST define event identity, ordering, and state-transition semantics sufficient for the stated replay guarantees.  A streaming interface MUST NOT be described as replayable merely because it emits events.  9. Security and Privacy  REQ-SEC-001 — Trust Boundaries  Implementations MUST document trust boundaries between application code, model providers, tools, stored context, and external services.  REQ-SEC-002 — Least Privilege  Tools and integrations MUST receive only the permissions required for their authorized operations.  REQ-SEC-003 — External Data Transmission  The handling of data transmitted to external providers MUST be documented, including applicable configuration controls and limitations.  REQ-SEC-004 — Sensitive Information  Logs, events, and diagnostic outputs MUST be designed to avoid unnecessary disclosure of credentials, secrets, and sensitive user data.  REQ-SEC-005 — Memory Controls  Where persistent memory is implemented, its retention behavior, access boundaries, and supported user controls MUST be documented.  REQ-SEC-006 — Security Verification  Security-sensitive behavior MUST be covered by appropriate tests or other documented verification evidence.  10. Validation and Error Handling  REQ-VAL-001 — Centralized Validation Policy  External input validation MUST follow the project’s documented validation architecture.  Where a central validation module is established as the authoritative boundary, modules MUST use that boundary rather than introduce inconsistent independent validation rules.  REQ-ERR-001 — Structured Errors  Core execution paths MUST expose errors through documented error contracts containing the context necessary for diagnosis.  REQ-ERR-002 — No Silent Failure  Errors MUST NOT be silently swallowed. Any recovery or retry behavior MUST be explicit, bounded, and documented.  11. Testing and Verification  REQ-TEST-001 — Execution Coverage  Automated tests MUST cover the principal execution paths, including successful execution, failure propagation, and termination behavior.  REQ-TEST-002 — State Verification  Tests MUST verify applicable state transitions and event-ordering guarantees.  REQ-TEST-003 — Tool Security  Tests MUST verify schema validation and authorization behavior for supported tool execution paths.  REQ-TEST-004 — Claims of Compliance  A component MUST NOT be described as compliant with this specification unless the applicable requirements have been assessed against implementation evidence.  ⸻  Part II — Architectural Guidance  The following statements express recommended engineering practices. They are not absolute requirements unless separately adopted as normative requirements.  12. Recommended Design Practices  12.1 Modular Architecture  Components SHOULD have a single, well-defined responsibility and SHOULD be independently testable where practical.  12.2 Stable Public APIs  Public APIs SHOULD expose stable, documented contracts and SHOULD avoid unnecessary breaking changes.  12.3 Type Safety  TypeScript implementations SHOULD use strict type checking, explicit result types, and discriminated unions where these improve correctness and readability.  12.4 Minimal Complexity  Implementations SHOULD prefer straightforward control flow, explicit dependencies, and the smallest architecture that satisfies verified requirements.  12.5 Documentation Maintenance  Requirements, public contracts, and implementation documentation SHOULD be maintained alongside the code they describe.  12.6 Provider Independence  The platform SHOULD minimize unnecessary coupling to any single provider, while acknowledging that providers may expose materially different capabilities and execution semantics.  ⸻  Part III — Future Intent  The items in this section describe strategic objectives. They are not normative requirements, delivery commitments, or statements of current implementation status.  13. Personal Intelligence  The long-term vision is to develop an integrated personal intelligence platform that can assist users across supported applications and environments.  Potential capabilities include contextual assistance, personalized interactions, delegated tasks, and coordinated access to authorized tools.  Each capability will require a defined scope, an implementation plan, and appropriate validation before it can be described as operational.  14. Local-First Intelligence  Future development MAY explore local model execution and local context processing where suitable hardware, models, and runtime environments are available.  The intended objectives include reducing unnecessary external data transmission, improving user control, and supporting operation in environments with limited connectivity.  Local execution does not automatically guarantee privacy, security, or equivalent model quality. These properties must be evaluated independently.  15. Multimodal Interaction  Future iterations MAY introduce or expand support for:  * Voice input and output. * Image and visual-content understanding. * Multimodal context management. * Accessible interaction across supported devices.  Support for each modality depends on the selected models, application permissions, platform capabilities, and verified integrations.  16. Application and Operating-System Integration  Future integrations MAY include iRiel AppWeb, native applications, Apple App Intents, Siri, Shortcuts, and other supported platform interfaces.  Each integration will require a separate assessment of API availability, authentication, authorization, privacy, and operating-system constraints.  The existence of an integration target does not establish that integration has been implemented.  17. Memory and Context Evolution  Future work MAY explore configurable memory retention, context summarization, user-controlled personalization, and portable context representations.  Any implementation must preserve the security and privacy boundaries defined by the applicable normative requirements.  18. Ecosystem Expansion  PRSL-AI MAY expand to include additional AI services, developer tools, application integrations, and shared capabilities.  Such expansion should preserve explicit contracts and independent component ownership rather than introduce implicit dependencies between projects.  19. Future Capability Acceptance Criteria  Before a future capability is promoted to an implemented feature, its development process SHOULD establish:  1. A documented scope and owner. 2. Explicit interface and security requirements. 3. An implementation plan. 4. Automated tests or equivalent verification. 5. Documented limitations and operational dependencies. 6. Updated user-facing and developer documentation.  Promotion from planned to implemented status MUST be based on evidence of implementation. Where operational verification remains incomplete, the capability MUST be identified as unverified.  ⸻  Part IV — Governance and Compliance  20. Requirement Lifecycle  Requirements SHOULD have stable identifiers so that they can be referenced in issues, pull requests, tests, and architecture reviews.  Changes to normative requirements SHOULD document the rationale, affected components, compatibility implications, and required verification updates.  Future intent SHOULD be maintained separately from binding requirements to prevent roadmap aspirations from becoming accidental implementation obligations.  21. Compliance Reporting  A compliance report SHOULD identify:  * The requirement identifier. * The affected component. * The implementation evidence. * The verification method. * The assessment result. * Known limitations or unresolved gaps.  Recommended assessment outcomes are:  * Pass: Sufficient evidence demonstrates compliance. * Fail: Available evidence demonstrates non-compliance. * Not Verified: Evidence is insufficient to establish compliance. * Not Applicable: The requirement does not apply to the assessed component, with justification.  22. Adoption and Authority  This document defines a proposed architectural baseline for PRSL-AI and iRiel AI.  Its normative requirements become authoritative only when adopted by the responsible project maintainers and applied to a clearly identified implementation scope.  Until that adoption and verification occur, the document must be treated as an architecture proposal rather than evidence of repository compliance.  23. Conclusion  PRSL-AI defines the ecosystem-level architectural context. iRiel AI defines the intelligence-platform context within that ecosystem.  Normative requirements establish the conditions implementations must satisfy. Architectural guidance recommends engineering practices. Future intent describes capabilities that may be developed as the ecosystem evolves.  Maintaining this distinction provides a clear basis for implementation, testing, security review, and roadmap planning without confusing architectural ambition with verified software behavior.  PRSL-AI establishes the ecosystem. iRiel AI delivers intelligence within it, subject to defined requirements and verified implementation.  ⸻  Maintained by Robert Software Labs.
author: iRiel-AI-Environment
